::: {.epigraph}
"A mathematician, like a painter or a poet, is a maker of patterns."

[— G. H. Hardy, *A Mathematician's Apology*]{.attribution}
:::

Here is a tiny act of vandalism.

Take the determinant of a $2 \times 2$ matrix:

$$
\det
\begin{pmatrix}
a & b \\
c & d
\end{pmatrix}
= ad - bc.
$$

Now erase the minus sign and write a plus sign instead:

$$
\operatorname{per}
\begin{pmatrix}
a & b \\
c & d
\end{pmatrix}
= ad + bc.
$$

That second expression is called the **permanent**. It looks like the
determinant's harmless cousin. Same products. Same entries. Same tiny formula.
Only the sign has changed.

But that sign is not punctuation. It is the trapdoor between two worlds.

The determinant is one of the most computable objects in mathematics. Gaussian
elimination finds it quickly, even for enormous matrices. The permanent, in
general, is one of the canonical hard counting problems. For $0$-$1$ matrices it
counts perfect matchings in a bipartite graph, and Valiant proved that computing
it exactly is $\#P$-complete [@valiant1979permanent].

So the question is not just "what is the difference?" The question is: how can a
minus sign carry that much power?

## Two ways to pair two rows

Start with the $2 \times 2$ case and forget matrices for a moment. Imagine two
workers and two jobs. The entry $a_{ij}$ is the weight, compatibility, or value
of assigning worker $i$ to job $j$.

There are exactly two perfect assignments:

$$
\begin{array}{ccl}
\text{straight pairing} &:& 1 \mapsto 1,\quad 2 \mapsto 2, \\
\text{crossed pairing}  &:& 1 \mapsto 2,\quad 2 \mapsto 1.
\end{array}
$$

The straight pairing contributes $ad$. The crossed pairing contributes $bc$.

The permanent adds both:

$$
\operatorname{per}
\begin{pmatrix}
a & b \\
c & d
\end{pmatrix}
= ad + bc.
$$

It asks: how much total weight is there across all perfect assignments?

The determinant also sees the same two assignments, but it gives one of them a
negative sign:

$$
\det
\begin{pmatrix}
a & b \\
c & d
\end{pmatrix}
= ad - bc.
$$

That negative sign is orientation. In the plane, the straight pairing keeps the
two basis directions in their original order; the crossed pairing swaps them.
Swapping two directions reverses orientation, and the determinant remembers that
reversal as a minus sign.

Already the personalities are different. The permanent is a census. The
determinant is a signed census, where oppositely oriented arrangements can cancel
each other out.

## The general formula

For an $n \times n$ matrix $A=(a_{ij})$, both formulas run over all permutations
of $\{1,\dots,n\}$. A permutation $\sigma$ chooses exactly one column
$\sigma(i)$ for each row $i$, and because $\sigma$ is a permutation, no two rows
choose the same column.

The permanent is

$$
\operatorname{per}(A)
=
\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}
\prod_{i=1}^n a_{i,\sigma(i)}.
$$ {#eq-permanent}

The determinant is

$$
\det(A)
=
\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}
\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)
\prod_{i=1}^n a_{i,\sigma(i)}.
$$ {#eq-determinant}

There it is: the same sum, except the determinant attaches the sign of the
permutation. Even permutations contribute positively. Odd permutations
contribute negatively.

If you have only seen determinants as row-reduction outputs, @eq-determinant may
look like a terrible way to compute them. It is. There are $n!$ permutations, and
$n!$ grows like an explosion with a clock attached. But the formula is the right
way to understand what the determinant is doing. It is collecting every possible
way the transformed basis vectors can contribute to oriented volume, then
letting opposite orientations cancel.

The permanent does the same collection without the orientation cancellation.

## What the determinant is allowed to forget

The determinant is not merely a formula. It is signed volume.

Put the columns of a matrix in space. They span a parallelogram in two
dimensions, a parallelepiped in three, and an $n$-dimensional volume in general.
The determinant tells you the signed size of that volume. Stretch a column, and
the volume stretches. Add one column to another, and the volume does not change,
because you have sheared the shape without changing its base-height content.
Swap two columns, and the orientation flips, so the sign changes.

These three habits are what make Gaussian elimination possible. The same rules
hold row-by-row as well as column-by-column, so row operations do not merely
manipulate entries; they manipulate signed volume in controlled ways. Shears
preserve it. Swaps flip its sign. Scaling a row scales it. By the end of
elimination, the matrix has been simplified to a triangular one, where the
volume is just the product of the diagonal entries.

So the determinant has a compression principle:

> Many different-looking matrices represent the same signed volume, and row
> reduction is allowed to move among them without losing the answer.

That is the algorithmic miracle. The determinant can forget enormous amounts of
detail because signed volume is an invariant. It does not need to remember every
assignment separately.

The permanent has no such mercy.

## What the permanent refuses to forget

Take a $0$-$1$ matrix and read it as the adjacency matrix of a bipartite graph.
Rows are workers, columns are jobs, and $a_{ij}=1$ means worker $i$ is allowed to
take job $j$.

For any permutation $\sigma$, the product

$$
\prod_{i=1}^n a_{i,\sigma(i)}
$$

is $1$ exactly when every chosen assignment is allowed, and $0$ otherwise.
Therefore @eq-permanent counts the number of perfect matchings in the graph:

$$
\operatorname{per}(A)
=
\#\{\text{perfect matchings of the bipartite graph}\}.
$$

This is the permanent's natural habitat. It counts how many global arrangements
survive local restrictions. That is why it appears in enumerative combinatorics
[@stanley2012].

Now compare what happens when two columns are equal.

For the determinant, equal columns force collapse. Geometrically, two basis
directions have landed on the same direction, so the volume is zero. Algebraically,
the terms in @eq-determinant pair off: swapping those two equal columns leaves
the product unchanged but reverses the sign. Every positive term meets an equal
negative term and disappears.

For the permanent, equal columns do not cancel. They reinforce. If two jobs have
identical compatibility patterns, the permanent sees two genuinely different
assignments. Worker 1 taking job A while worker 2 takes job B is not the same as
worker 1 taking job B while worker 2 takes job A, even if the columns look
identical. The permanent says: count both.

This is the heart of the matter.

The determinant turns symmetry into cancellation. The permanent turns symmetry
into multiplicity.

## The all-ones matrix

Here is the cleanest place to feel the difference. Let $J_n$ be the $n \times n$
matrix whose entries are all $1$.

Every worker can do every job. How many perfect assignments are there?

There are $n!$, one for each permutation, so

$$
\operatorname{per}(J_n) = n!.
$$

The permanent sees the full combinatorial abundance.

But the determinant sees something else:

$$
\det(J_n) = 0
\qquad \text{for } n\ge 2.
$$

All columns are identical. As vectors, they span only a line. The $n$-dimensional
volume has collapsed completely. The determinant does not care that there are
many assignments; it cares that the transformed coordinate directions do not
enclose any volume.

This example is almost unfairly revealing. The same matrix is either maximally
rich or completely degenerate, depending on the question.

The permanent asks, "How many ways can the choices be matched?"

The determinant asks, "How much oriented space do these columns enclose?"

Those are not two versions of the same question. They only wear the same
notation.

## Why the sign makes computation easier

It is tempting to say that the determinant is easy because subtraction allows
cancellation, while the permanent is hard because all permutation signs are
positive. That is close, but it needs sharpening.

Subtraction alone is not magic. The magic is that the determinant's cancellations
are structured. They are exactly the cancellations required by geometry:

- If two columns agree, the determinant must be zero.
- If one column is a sum of two columns, the volume splits linearly.
- If one column is changed by adding a multiple of another, the volume is unchanged.
- If two columns swap places, the orientation reverses.

These rules are so rigid that they determine the determinant. More importantly,
they let an algorithm take shortcuts. Gaussian elimination can kill entries one
at a time because it knows which operations preserve signed volume and which
operations change it in simple ways.

The permanent does not behave like volume. In the matching interpretation,
adding one row to another does not preserve the number of matchings. Swapping
columns does not introduce an orientation sign. Two equal columns do not make
the answer vanish. The permanent is not an invariant of a shape being sheared
through space. In its $0$-$1$ form, it is a count of discrete choices, and counts
are stubborn. If there are a million possible matchings, the permanent is trying
to account for a million possible matchings.

This is why the naive formula is misleading in opposite directions.

For the determinant, the $n!$-term formula looks hard, but the object has hidden
geometry that lets us compress the computation.

For the permanent, the $n!$-term formula looks similar, but the object is
genuinely asking a counting question with no comparable general compression
known. Valiant's theorem says this is not an accident of our imagination: even
for $0$-$1$ matrices, exact permanent computation captures the difficulty of
$\#P$ counting problems [@valiant1979permanent].

## A small warning about slogans

"The permanent is hard because it has no minus signs" is a useful first
sentence, but it is not the whole explanation.

There are special families where permanent-like counts become tractable. Planar
matching problems, for example, can sometimes be smuggled back into a
determinant or Pfaffian after choosing signs with great care; the dimer-counting
story behind domino tilings is one beautiful example. We already touched that
world in the domino post.

The deeper slogan is this:

> Signs are useful when they encode structure.

In the determinant, permutation signs encode orientation. That orientation gives
the determinant its geometric meaning, its cancellation laws, and its fast
algorithms. In the permanent, replacing every permutation sign by $+$ destroys
that orientation. What remains is not a bad determinant. It is a different
creature: a pure count of compatible global choices.

## Why this belongs in linear algebra

At first, the permanent sounds like combinatorics and the determinant sounds like
linear algebra. That is true, but too neat.

The determinant sits at a crossing point. It is a polynomial in the matrix
entries, a volume measurement, a test for invertibility, and a signed sum over
permutations. Linear algebra usually teaches the volume and invertibility
stories. Combinatorics notices the sum over permutations. Algorithms notice the
gap between the two formulas.

The permanent forces all three perspectives into the same room. It asks:

> What part of the determinant's power came from the products, and what part came
> from the signs?

The answer is bracing. The products alone give you assignments. The signs give
you orientation. Orientation gives you cancellation. Cancellation gives you a
geometry. Geometry gives you fast computation.

Remove the signs, and you do not get a simpler determinant. You get the permanent:
an object that remembers every compatible arrangement and refuses to let opposite
terms annihilate each other.

## What to remember

The determinant and the permanent are built from the same permutation products.
The determinant weights each product by the sign of the permutation; the
permanent gives every product a plus sign.

That small formal difference changes the meaning completely. The determinant is
signed volume, so its terms cancel in exactly the ways geometry demands. Those
cancellations make row reduction possible and let us compute it quickly. The
permanent is a counting function. For a $0$-$1$ matrix, it counts perfect
matchings in a bipartite graph. It has no orientation to exploit, no general
Gaussian-elimination shortcut, and exact computation is $\#P$-complete.

So the minus sign in the determinant is not a nuisance. It is the reason the
determinant is a geometric object rather than just an enormous sum.
